answer.exemplar: Factoring turns two different-looking problems into one pattern, and the pattern is the same in both. A divisor of a number is fixed by choosing, for each prime, an exponent between 0 and the exponent in the factorisation, so 360 written as 2 to the power 3 times 3 to the power 2 times 5 gives 4 times 3 times 2, which is 24 divisors, a figure that no amount of direct trial division produces as cleanly. A least common multiple is the same idea read the other way: 24 as 2 to the power 3 times 3 and 36 as 2 to the power 2 times 3 to the power 2 give 2 to the power 3 times 3 to the power 2, which is 72, where taking the product and dividing by the gcd of 12 gives the same answer by a longer route. There is also a checking value, because the factored form exposes errors at a glance: a factorisation whose exponents do not reproduce the original number is wrong before any counting begins. The honest limit is that factoring is itself work, so for a single small division test it is not worth it, and a misread factorisation propagates into every later answer.

questions.explanation: A strong answer shows the shared structure rather than only asserting that factoring is faster, for instance by pointing out that the divisor count and the least common multiple are both read off the same list of prime powers, with 360 giving 24 divisors and 24 with 36 giving a least common multiple of 72. It should also credit the diagnostic role, since a factorisation that does not multiply back to the original number is caught immediately. A weaker answer will only say factoring is easier, which leaves out the reason it is easier, and the strongest will say when it is not worth doing at all.

questions.explanation: A complete graph on n vertices has n to the power n minus 2 spanning trees, so for 5 vertices that is 5 to the power 3, which is 125. The formula is worth knowing rather than deriving, and it is worth checking on a small case, since a complete graph on 3 vertices is a triangle and has 3 spanning trees, and 3 to the power 1 is 3. Every spanning tree here uses 4 of the 10 edges, so a brute-force search would examine all 210 sets of 4 edges and keep the 125 that reach every vertex without closing a circuit.

questions.explanation: Start from the connected graph and remove one edge from any circuit that is present. Doing so cannot disconnect the graph, because the rest of the circuit still provides a route between the two ends of the removed edge, and the process ends when no circuit remains, which is exactly a tree. Since no vertex was discarded on the way, the result reaches all 7 vertices and is therefore a spanning tree. Connectivity is the hypothesis this argument needs, and without it a tree on all the vertices may not exist at all, since some vertices could be stranded in separate pieces.

edges = {"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["A", "C", "D"], "C": ["A", "B"], "D": ["B"]}
seen = set()
order = []

def walk(v):
    if v in seen:
        return
    seen.add(v)
    order.append(v)
    for nxt in edges[v]:
        walk(nxt)
